Lessons.Title: Make Sense of Decimal Addition PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 U05:L11 Make Sense of Decimal Addition PLC Activity: decimal addends are amounts of SAME whole-unit hundredths, and learner may use partial sums, a grid, or compensation. Composing100 hundredths produces one whole. Source expects a pupil-generated algorithm and explanation BEFORE formalizing any one standard procedure.

Warm-up How Many Do You See Grids: first two original hundredths grids shade20 and90 cells, corresponding0.20+0.90=1.10 (one whole plus10 hundredths); next two shade95 and7 cells ->0.95+0.07=1.02; third pair20 and9 cells ->0.20+0.09=0.29. Original source alt-descriptions explicitly reveal cell counts; they were not the invented68/37 previously in Rich V2.

Activity1 The Sum: original numerical prompt is2.26+1.87=4.13. Show own strategy e.g2+1=3 and0.26+0.87=1.13 then compose to4.13, or2.26+1.74=4 then+0.13. Teacher reviews student diagrams and mathematical explanation, not just the exact selected option.

Activity2 Target Numbers Add Tenths or Hundredths: both partners start at0, roll the number cube, decide whether to add drawn number of TENTHS or HUNDREDTHS, keep a running total for SIX turns and aim as CLOSE to1 AS POSSIBLE WITHOUT EXCEEDING1. There is no fixed winning total; original dice results, independent moves and discussion of alternate move require TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Prior fictional six-turn sequence remains separately labeled extension, not publisher source sequence.

Source's original warmup images, student-created strategies and game score cannot be inferred from a digital exact-answer option. An independent Edulytiks Cool-down asks pupils to find1.48+2.67=4.15 and explain regrouping, distinct from gated original.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: make sense of decimal addition by choosing and explaining a strategy before formalizing the standard algorithm. The original 2021 lesson starts with How Many Do You See hundredths-grid images and then has students make gallery-walk displays of their independently chosen addition approach.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up — count shaded hundredths: describe two original complete unit-square grids, one with 68 hundredth cells shaded and another with 37. Combine 68+37=105 hundredths, meaning one whole and five hundredths. Students may regroup 32 shaded parts from the second model to finish the first whole; they must identify the same full square unit in both grids.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — show a strategy: calculate 3.48+2.76 using a hundredths-grid picture, expanded notation, compensation or an original student-selected approach. A place-value explanation is 3+2=5 wholes, 0.4+0.7=1.1 and 0.08+0.06=0.14; regroup to 6.24. A second valid method moves 0.52 from 2.76 to complete the first addend to 4 and adds the remaining 2.24. Prepare an accessible explanation or visual to compare strategies with partners.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — Target Numbers variation: begin at zero; with a supplied sequence of six digit-card values 2,3,4,1,5,2, choose each as tenths or hundredths. Try to reach the largest total not exceeding one. One valid sequence of values 0.2,0.3,0.04,0.1,0.05,0.02 totals 0.71. Students must review why a different set of tenths/hundredths choices may make a better total and write equations for all six steps; never claim this single demonstration is the winning strategy.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: the source's peer display, mathematical questions, six decisions, and explanation of how a decision changes the outcome are open tasks. A numeric decimal addition check is a supporting Practice item only, not proof that a six-turn partner game or gallery discussion was completed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decimal units compose
KeyConcepts.Definition: Ten hundredths become one tenth, and ten tenths become one whole.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 0.68+0.37=1.05 because 105 hundredths make a whole plus five hundredths.
KeyConcepts.Example: The grid has one hundred equal parts per unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple valid addition methods
KeyConcepts.Definition: Add quantities by place value, by regrouped pictures or by compensation while preserving the total.
KeyConcepts.Example: Moving 0.52 from the second addend to the first changes the summands but not the sum.

KeyConcepts.Title: Game objective and constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: Six selected decimal increments are added to a running total, with the final total no greater than 1.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 0≤sum≤1; compare final totals and seek the closest allowed value to 1.
KeyConcepts.Example: A learner must explain which place-value choices improved their attempt.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source three hundredths grid pairs
WorkedExamples.Question: Find20+90,95+7,20+9 shaded HUNDREDTH units from same whole.
WorkedExamples.Method: Combine cell counts in hundredth-grid units, composing one whole when at least100.
Steps: 20+90=110 hundredths=1.10.
95+7=102 hundredths=1.02.
20+9=29 hundredths=0.29.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source2.26+1.87
WorkedExamples.Question: Find2.26+1.87 and explain a chosen decimal strategy.
WorkedExamples.Method: Combine aligned place-value components or use compensation.
Steps: The original1.87 has0.13 still left.
Final sum4.13; alternatively0.26+0.87=1.13.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source strategy and presentation teacher reviewed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Target Numbers six-turn partner game
WorkedExamples.Question: Describe how six turns of tenths-or-hundredths dice addition can approach1 without exceeding.
WorkedExamples.Method: Each round has a number cube result and student-selected decimal unit.
Steps: Both begin0 and roll source number cube.
On each turn choose tenths or hundredths, recording running sum.
After six rounds compare closest non-exceeding totals and explain a revisable move.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Open player-specific totals; no one fixed source win.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher assesses game journal and reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Compose shaded hundredths
WorkedExamples.Question: Two unit grids show 68 and 37 shaded hundredths. What is the combined amount?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Count 68 hundredths in the first whole and 37 in the second.
Combine to 105 hundredths.
Regroup 100 hundredths as one whole and retain five hundredths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Choose a method
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 3.48+2.76 in at least two mathematically compatible ways.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Use decimal-place sums: 3+2, 4/10+7/10, and 8/100+6/100.
Compose the 11 tenths and 14 hundredths into equivalent larger places.
Alternatively shift 0.52 from 2.76 to 3.48 and add 4+2.24.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Record a six-choice attempt
WorkedExamples.Question: A player chooses 0.2,0.3,0.04,0.1,0.05,0.02 in six turns. Does the total exceed 1?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Add tenths first: 0.2+0.3+0.1=0.6.
Combine 0.6+0.11 and compare to one.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The total is 0.71, so it does not exceed 1.
WorkedExamples.Check: The six-turn record must be checked for one choice per supplied digit, and teacher reviews strategy.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat ten hundredths as a new whole
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Ten hundredths make a tenth; one hundred hundredths make a whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Regroup each place at exactly ten of the next smaller unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Automatically mark the numeric score as the full game
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A strategy game also asks for six legal choices, a partner comparison and a proposed revision.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the full move record, reflect on a changed move and retain teacher assessment.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Present fictional68/37 shaded grids and3.48+2.76 as original 2021 Activity numbers
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original printed source has20/90,95/7,20/9 grid counts and2.26+1.87 exact addends.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore source grid/shaded sums and original addition while retaining unrelated correct work only as extensions.

SummaryPoints: Source Activity1 2.26+1.87=4.13 with multiple valid pupil strategies.
Source six-round game uses self-selected tenths/hundredths and variable rolls, not a fixed answer.
Learner-written explanation, original grid images and partner game are teacher reviewed.
Selected numeric choice is limited to three known source grid sums and one original sum.
Optional prior: Decimal addition can be justified through area models, composed units or compensation.
Optional prior: The original game has a six-turn place-value choice and cannot be replaced by one sum.
Optional prior: Teacher reviews student diagrams, partner discussion and explanation of strategy.

Lessons.Title: Estimate and Add
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: estimate decimal sums and organize an addition standard algorithm with each decimal place aligned, composing tenths and whole units as necessary. In the 2021 source, students first find a decimal sum their own way, critique another learner's algorithm after partner feedback, and only then estimate sums whose decimal-place counts differ.

Warm-up: use a benchmark such as 4.70+3.20≈8 and discuss why the actual sum is close to 8 before calculating; an estimate is an early magnitude check, not a substitute for exact result or justifying its precision.

Activity 1 — connect strategies: calculate 4.76+2.58 as 4.76+2.00+0.58=7.34. Then write vertical columns, align both decimal points and compose 6+8=14 hundredths into one tenth and four hundredths. Continue adding tenths with the carry, explain why the final sum is 7.34, and revise a partner explanation if it confuses the composed unit.

Activity 2 — decimal lengths differ: estimate 3.7+6.84. Write 3.70+6.84=10.54, close to 11. Next estimate 8.96+2.3 by comparison with 9+2.3≈11.3, then calculate 8.96+2.30=11.26. Compare these estimates to whole numbers and explain why right-aligning the last *printed digits* can add hundredths to tenths incorrectly.

Assessment: exact sums and nearest-whole decisions can be checked, but teacher reviews the algorithm's carry explanation, initial estimate, learner choice of method and revision after partner questions. Source student-response and protected Cool-down not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Align equal place values
KeyConcepts.Definition: Decimal addition columns align whole units, tenths and hundredths, not the last printed digit.
KeyConcepts.Example: Missing hundredths in a short decimal may be represented as zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compose a new unit
KeyConcepts.Definition: Ten hundredths become one tenth, possibly affecting the tenths sum and whole sum.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate before exact result
KeyConcepts.Definition: Round or compensate to predict the approximate whole-number magnitude.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 3.7+6.84 is close to 11, and exact result 10.54 is nearer 11 than 10.
KeyConcepts.Example: An estimate and an exact sum have different epistemic roles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain decimal composing
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 4.76+2.58 with a correctly aligned algorithm.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Add 6 hundredths+8 hundredths=14 hundredths; write 4 and carry one tenth.
Add 7 tenths+5 tenths+1 tenth=13 tenths; write 3 tenths and carry one whole.
Add 4+2+1 whole and record the decimal alignment.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate and align
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate 3.7+6.84 and calculate exactly.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Estimate by 3.7≈4 and 6.84≈7, giving a nearby total of 11.
Write 3.70 so the hundredths columns align.
Add to obtain the exact sum.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use compensation
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 8.96+2.3 without dropping the missing hundredth.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Use 2.3=2.30 and add by aligned columns.
Or round 8.96 up to 9 by adding 0.04 and remove that from 2.30.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Right-align the final numeral character instead of the decimal points
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A tenths digit from one operand must not add directly to a hundredths digit from another.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align decimal places and pad a missing hundredths digit with zero.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forget a composed tenth when adding a hundredths carry
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Fourteen hundredths contain one more tenth and four hundredths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Carry the one tenth into the correct next place.

SummaryPoints: Estimate sums using sensible whole-number benchmarks before exact computation.
Place-value alignment and composed-unit explanation are central to the algorithm.
Teacher reviews why students' method and peer revisions are valid.

Lessons.Title: Analyze Addition Mistakes
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: CRITIQUE AND CORRECT incorrect addition strategies when two decimals have different numbers of printed decimal digits. The 2021 source's core misconception is treating whole-number right alignment as valid for decimals, then judging a wrong result only because it is slightly larger than one addend.

Warm-up: compare expressions such as 42.8+6.15 and 4.28+61.5 and explain why the same digit strings can describe very different magnitudes; write them as aligned place-value quantities before computing.

Activity 1 — analyze a fictional student: one learner writes 518.37+64.2 as 524.79 after lining up last digits, treating 2 tenths as two hundredths. Another writes 518.37+64.20=582.57 by aligning decimal points. Use benchmark 520+60≈580 to refute the implausibly small 524.79, identify the exact incorrect columns, and explain why the correct total is 582.57. Teacher reviews the critique, not merely the number.

Activity 2 — same digit groups, different place values: find 4.82+6.37=11.19; 48.2+63.7=111.9; 482+6.37=488.37; and 48.2+6.37=54.57. Each uses similar digits but shifts their place values. Draw a decimal-position table and compare strategies using all needed trailing-zero placeholders.

Assessment: it is not enough to choose the learner with the correct number; the source asks learners to explain the specific place-value misalignment, use an estimate to detect it, revise an argument and compare several mixed-precision sums. Teacher adjudicates critique and mathematical communication.

KeyConcepts.Title: Magnitude exposes impossible sums
KeyConcepts.Definition: A result should be consistent with a rough benchmark before checking individual digits.
KeyConcepts.Example: 524.79 is implausibly small because it adds only around 6 instead of 64.

KeyConcepts.Title: Align decimals and equal units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Add hundreds to hundreds, tens to tens, tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Right alignment of printed digits is incorrect for unequal decimal lengths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same digits can mean different magnitudes
KeyConcepts.Definition: Place value changes the quantity even if the printed digits look familiar.
KeyConcepts.Example: The number of whole units changes across examples.

WorkedExamples.Title: Critique a false answer
WorkedExamples.Question: A pupil says 518.37+64.2=524.79. What went wrong?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Benchmark the total near 580, making 524.79 suspicious.
Write 64.2 as 64.20 and align decimal points under 518.37.
Add columns to get 582.57; identify the wrong place-value pairing in the pupil's work.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews whether the learner explains the exact column error.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same digits, different scale
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 4.82+6.37 and 48.2+63.7.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: For the first, combine hundredths, tenths and units.
For the second, combine tenths, units and tens.
Compare their magnitudes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mixed whole and decimal
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 482+6.37 without right-aligning the last printed digits.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original decimal place-value explanation with an independently checkable numerical result; diagram and peer discourse require teacher assessment.
Steps: Write 482 as 482.00 to align decimals.
Add hundredths and tenths to the zero placeholders.
Add whole-number parts.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Align the rightmost digit of unequal-length decimals
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Whole-number alignment discards the meaning of the decimal-point positions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align decimal points, not final digits, and verify a place-value chart.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accept any result slightly greater than the larger addend
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The second addend may add dozens or hundreds of units, not just a positive fraction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use an independent approximate sum to check whether the result is reasonable.

SummaryPoints: The standard algorithm is correct only when like decimal units are combined.
A place-value explanation is required to critique a mistaken calculation.
Estimating supports diagnosis but does not replace a complete correction.
